h1: Should Your Office Sponsor a Student? An Honest Look at the Math
lead: Every few weeks a dentist or office manager in East Texas asks some version of the same question: if we help put someone through school, do we get an assistant out of it? Here is the straight answer, including the parts that argue against it.
lead_heading: Thinking about sponsoring? Ask Amanda anything first.

sections.html:
A sponsorship is a business paying some or all of one student's tuition at Premier Dental Academy so that person can train as a dental assistant. That is the whole mechanism. There is no contract binding the student to your office, no repayment schedule hanging over her, and no employment agreement stapled to the money.

We invoice your business directly and apply every dollar to that student's tuition account. You can cover a full seat or any part of one — current amounts live on the sponsor a student page, which reads from the same payment system as checkout, so it is never out of date the way a blog post can be.

It is not a donation. Premier Dental Academy is a private career school, not a 501(c)(3) charity. A sponsorship is not a charitable contribution, and we will never describe it as one — including on the invoice.

sections.h2: The math starts with what you are not buying
sections.html:
This is the part most schools skip, so we will lead with it. Sponsoring a student does not buy you an employee. Your student is free to interview anywhere when she finishes, including at offices that never wrote a check. She is not obligated to apply with you, accept an offer from you, or stay a certain length of time.

Any program that tells an office otherwise is selling something it cannot deliver, and we would rather lose the sponsorship than pretend.

What we will never promise you: a hire, a start date, a wage, a specific student's outcome, or that any sponsored student finishes the program. If your student stops attending, we will tell you before anything else happens with the funds.

So what does the money actually buy? Three real things. A person from this area gets trained who otherwise would not have. Your business is recognized publicly as her sponsor, with her permission and yours. And you get a genuine first look — you know her name, her town, and her progress months before she ever posts a resume.

The offices that sponsor are usually not doing charity math. They are doing labor-market math. In a market this size, waiting for an experienced assistant to appear on a job board means waiting behind every other practice in Gregg, Smith, and Harrison counties for the same small pool of people. Growing one is slower, but it is a supply you influence rather than a queue you stand in.

The second reason is fit. An assistant trained locally, who already knows the towns your patients drive in from, tends to settle in rather than treat the job as a stop. We wrote about what East Texas offices actually value in a new graduate in why East Texas offices hire PDA graduates, and the broader tradeoff in train someone or hire experienced.

The third reason is the least businesslike and the most commonly cited out loud: somebody in your town wants this badly and cannot cover tuition, and you can fix that with a decision you make in an afternoon.

sections.h2: Reasons to say no this year
sections.html:
A sponsorship is a bad idea for plenty of practices, and we would rather you skip it than resent it. Say no if any of these are true.

You need someone in the chair next month. Training runs about twelve weeks, and state registration is a separate process the student handles afterward with the Texas State Board of Dental Examiners. Sponsorship is a next-season move, not a staffing emergency fix.

You want a guarantee. There is not one, and there will not be one. If the only version of this you would accept is a binding commitment from the student, this is not for you.

The cost would strain the quarter. Tuition money is applied immediately and is not a line you want to be nervous about. There is no penalty for waiting a cohort.

Cheaper ways to be involved. You can request a graduate when you are hiring, or host a student for externship hours — here is what that involves. Both cost nothing and both put you in front of students earlier than a job posting would.

sections.h2: The tax question, answered the only honest way
sections.html:
We get asked whether a sponsorship is a write-off, and the honest answer is that we are a dental assisting school, not your accountant.

Here are the facts we can state. Premier Dental Academy is a private career school, not a 501(c)(3), so a sponsorship is not a charitable donation. We invoice your business directly and provide full documentation showing exactly what was paid and which student's tuition it was applied to. Many local businesses treat a sponsorship as an ordinary business expense in the same family as advertising or workforce development, particularly given the public recognition that comes with it.

Whether that treatment fits your situation depends on your entity, your books, and your year. Ask your CPA. Anyone who answers that question for you without seeing your return is guessing.

sections.h2: What actually happens after you say yes
sections.html:
The process is deliberately low-tech, because it runs on Amanda talking to people.

Students who want the class but cannot cover tuition apply through the form on the sponsorship page. Amanda speaks with every one of them personally. With each student's written consent, a short first-name-only profile goes on the board — nothing about anyone appears publicly without their written okay.

You either pick a student from the board or tell Amanda what matters to you — your town, a single parent restarting, someone your office already knows — and she matches you. We invoice your business, apply the funds to that student's tuition, and she enrolls in the next cohort on the calendar.

From there she trains at the Longview campus with real equipment and real instruments in a class capped at eight, and when she finishes we help her interview with East Texas offices. You will know how the story ends, which is more than most workforce spending can say.

sections.h2: If a full seat is more than you want to commit
sections.html:
Partial sponsorships are common and genuinely useful. Covering a student's down payment is often the exact thing standing between someone and a start date, and any amount goes straight onto a tuition account rather than into overhead. Two offices splitting a seat happens too.

If you want to talk it through before committing to anything, call or text Amanda at (903) 913-6444. She runs the school, she knows every student on that board by name, and she can tell you in one conversation whether there is currently someone who fits what you had in mind.

And if you landed here as a future student rather than an employer: this program exists for you, and applying costs nothing. Start at the sponsorship page or just apply to the program and tell us what is in the way.
